hook: Mrs. Lee, 68, collapses at a bus stop and is not breathing. A bystander kneels, puts the heel of one hand on the lower half of her breastbone, and pushes hard and fast. With each push, the front of her chest sinks about 5 cm and then springs back. Her rib cage can do that because its front ends are cartilage, not bone. Knowing its parts tells you where to push and what can break.

prereq.q: What kind of cartilage is flexible and smooth, and covers the ends of bones?
prereq.why: Hyaline cartilage is smooth and bends slightly, and it covers bone ends. The costal cartilages of the ribs are made of it too. Fibrocartilage forms the intervertebral discs, and elastic cartilage shapes the outer ear.

prereq.q: How many thoracic vertebrae does an adult have?
prereq.why: There are 12 thoracic vertebrae, T1 to T12, one for each pair of ribs. There are 7 cervical and 5 lumbar vertebrae.
Thoracic vertebrae have costal facets, the smooth pits where the ribs meet them. Cervical vertebrae have transverse foramina instead, and lumbar vertebrae have neither.

anatomy.caption: The sternum and the thoracic cage from the front. Hide the labels, name the three parts of the sternum and its landmarks, then count the ribs down from the sternal angle.

chain.cause: Each rib's head and tubercle meet the thoracic vertebrae at the back.
chain.effect: The rib can swing up and down around its back end, like the handle of a bucket.

chain.cause: At the front, each rib continues as a costal cartilage of hyaline cartilage, joined to the sternum directly or through the cartilage above.
chain.effect: The front of the cage can bend and twist instead of being held rigid.

chain.cause: When muscles lift the ribs, their curved bodies swing outward and the sternum moves forward.
chain.effect: The cage widens from side to side and from front to back.

chain.cause: When the force stops, the bent costal cartilages spring back to their resting shape.
chain.effect: The cage returns to its resting size, which is also what lets the chest recoil after each CPR compression.

misconception.wrong: Floating ribs are loose ribs that are not attached to anything.
misconception.right: Floating ribs (11 and 12) are attached at the back, where their heads meet the vertebrae, just like every other rib. What they lack is a front attachment: their short cartilages end in the muscles of the abdominal wall instead of reaching the sternum. "Floating" describes only the front end.

summary: The thoracic cage is the 12 thoracic vertebrae, 12 pairs of ribs with their costal cartilages, and the sternum. The sternum has a manubrium, a body and a xiphoid process; the jugular notch is at its top, and the sternal angle marks the second rib, which is how ribs are counted. A rib has a head that meets two vertebral bodies, a neck, a tubercle that meets a transverse process, an angle, a body and a costal groove that shelters a nerve and vessels. Ribs 1 to 7 are true ribs, 8 to 12 are false ribs, and 11 and 12 are floating ribs with no front attachment. The costal cartilages make the cage flexible.
